\section[\ar{من} \ar{فضلك}]{\ar{من} \ar{فضلك} (min faḍlik) — please}

\label{lesson:AR-C06-min-fadlik}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Arabic doesn't say "please" — it asks for something \emph{from your grace.}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The phrase}
\textbf{\ar{من} \ar{فضلك}} — read right to left, \textbf{min faḍlik} — is two pieces:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{من}} (\emph{min}, "from") + \textbf{\ar{فضلك}} (\emph{faḍl} + \emph{-ik/-ak}, "your grace/bounty") $\to$ "\textbf{from your grace.}"
\end{quote}

\emph{faḍl} is a warm, weighty word — "grace, favour, bounty, generosity" (you'll meet it as the name \emph{Faḍl}). Saying \emph{min faḍlik} casts the request as drawing on the other person's generosity — not a command, a courtesy.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens — A gender note (Arabic marks "you")}]
The ending changes with \textbf{whom you address} — and, unwritten, only the vowel moves:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item to a \textbf{woman}: \emph{min faḍl\textbf{ik}} (the \ar{ك} said \emph{-ik})
  \item to a \textbf{man}: \emph{min faḍl\textbf{ak}} (the \ar{ك} said \emph{-ak})
\end{itemize}

The spelling \textbf{\ar{فضلك}} is the same for both; the short vowel that distinguishes them isn't normally written. One sound to respect: the \textbf{\ar{ض}} (\emph{ḍ}) is an \textbf{emphatic} d, said with a heavier, deeper tongue than a plain \emph{d}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Another everyday "please"}
Just as common, especially getting someone's attention:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{لو} \ar{سمحت}} — \emph{law samaḥt} — literally "\textbf{if you permit}" (\emph{law} "if" + \emph{samaḥt} "you permitted"). Same politeness, a different image — permission rather than grace.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "min faḍlik" — feel the heavy \ar{ض}{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: taken apart — "from your grace"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the alternative — "law samaḥt" = "if you permit"{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} How do you say please in Arabic? (\textbf{min faḍlik}, \ar{من} \ar{فضلك}.) What does it literally mean? ("\textbf{From your grace}" — \emph{faḍl} = grace/bounty.) What changes between saying it to a man vs a woman? (The \ar{ك} ending — \emph{-ak} to a man, \emph{-ik} to a woman; spelling unchanged.) What's the other common "please," and what does it mean? (\textbf{law samaḥt} — "if you permit.")
\end{tcolorbox}
